segments.text: Explain why prices go up to a 10-year-old

baseline_runs.answer: Imagine your favorite candy bar is the last one left in the store, and three kids all want it! They'd probably offer more money to get it. Stores know that, so they raise the price. When lots of people want something and there isn't enough to go around, prices go up. That's called supply and demand!

Imagine your favorite candy bar costs $1, but then lots of kids want it and there aren't many left in the store. The store can charge more, maybe $1.50, because people really want it. When lots of people want something and there isn't enough to go around, prices go up. When there's plenty, prices can come down!

Imagine your favorite candy bar costs $1. If lots of kids want it, but the shop only has a few left, the shopkeeper might raise the price to 2 dollars. Why? Because more kids are willing to pay more to get one! When things are in high demand but short supply, prices usually go up. That's how it works for almost everything.

If there are only 10 bars and 30 kids want one, the kids who really want it might offer more money, so the price rises. When more candy is made, the price can come back down.

Prices go up when more people want something than there is to go around. Imagine a candy bar that everyone at school suddenly wants, but the store only has five left. Kids start offering their allowance to get one, so the shop owner raises the price. Higher prices slow down how many people buy it and encourage the shop to order more candy.

runs.answer: Imagine you have a bag of 10 candies, and you give 3 to your friend. How many candies do you have left? Just subtract: 10 minus 3 equals 7! You still have 7 sweet treats to enjoy. Subtraction is simply taking away, and once you practice with candy, you'll be a pro in no time. Keep up the great work!

Imagine you have five candies, and your friend gives you three more. Now you have eight candies in total! That's addition: when we combine groups, we add them together. Try it yourself: if you have four gummy bears and get two more, how many do you have? Keep up the great work!

ablations.prompt: You are a friendly teacher. Explain why prices go up to a 10-year-old with a candy example.

runs.answer:
Okay, let's pretend we run a candy stand together! Let's say you sell lollipops for 50 cents each.

Now, imagine that suddenly *everybody* in town wants lollipops. Maybe there's a big parade coming, and all the kids want a treat. You'd have tons of customers lining up, but you only have 20 lollipops left in your box.

What do you think you'd do? Many people would be willing to pay a little more to get one of those last lollipops, right? So you might raise the price to 75 cents. Some kids might decide it's not worth it and skip buying one, which is fine. But the lollipops you have go to the people who want them most.

That's the basic idea of why prices go up: **when more people want something than there is available, the price tends to rise.** The higher price also helps balance things out, because some people decide to wait or buy something else instead.

Now the other side: if you suddenly had a huge box of 500 lollipops and nobody wanted them, what would you do with the price? You'd probably lower it to attract customers!

So prices are kind of like a conversation between buyers and sellers, where how much people want something and how much of it there is both matter.

Can you think of something in your own life where you've noticed a price going up or down?

Okay, imagine you and your friends LOVE a certain candy bar. Let's say it's called the Super Crunch Bar.

Now, at the store, there are only 10 Super Crunch Bars left on the shelf. Suddenly, 30 kids all want to buy one! What happens? The store owner notices that everybody wants them, but there aren't enough to go around. So the owner might say, "Hey, these are really popular, so I'm going to raise the price a little!"

Why would they do that? Because some kids would still really want the candy and be willing to pay more for it. And if the price goes up, some kids who weren't sure might decide to buy something else instead. That way, the 10 candy bars get shared out among the kids who want them most.

Now flip it around. Imagine the Super Crunch Bar is old news, and nobody really wants it anymore. The store has 50 bars sitting there. The owner wants to sell them, so they lower the price to get kids interested again.

So here's the big idea: when lots of people want something and there isn't much of it, the price goes up. When there's plenty of it and not many people want it, the price goes down. That's how prices work for almost everything, not just candy!

Pretty cool, right?
